Notes: First documented Jewish presence. c. 580 BCE (year assigned by the compiler: Jeremiah 44 is set shortly after the flight of Judeans to Egypt that followed the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BCE and the murder of Gedaliah). The Jewish Encyclopedia (s.v. Memphis), citing Jer. 44:1 and 46:14, says that Jews fleeing the Babylonian war to Egypt had formed a colony at Memphis (Hebrew Noph). Jer. 44:1 addresses 'all the Judeans living in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros'. This shows a refugee community of unknown size. No number is given. Basis for Year Established: this biblical attestation.

Persian period, late 6th through 5th c. BCE (midpoint c. -462). Encyclopaedia Judaica (s.v. Papyri) says that the earliest Jewish papyri from Egypt, in Aramaic and dating from the late 6th through the 5th c. BCE, were found at several sites including Memphis, as well as Elephantine and Hermopolis Magna. The entry does not identify the Memphis texts or their Jewish content. Caution: Szántó (2016 dissertation, citing Thompson 1988 p. 85) notes that Jews may have served as mercenaries in Memphis under the Persians but that there is 'no decisive evidence'. The Hermopolis letters sent from Memphis are generally considered Aramean (pagan), not Jewish. Population blank.

c. 250 BCE (papyrus dated 275-226 BCE; midpoint). SB XXIV 16272 (P. Cairo inv. JE 51509; Galazzi & Sijpesteijn, ZPE 113, 1996) from Saqqara, the necropolis of Memphis, is a list of daily incomes and payments containing one 'certainly Jewish name, Annaios'. Szántó calls this 'only scanty evidence for the presence of Jews in Memphis' and says literary sources 'remain silent about the Jews in Memphis'. Evidence of at least one individual. Not counted as Memphis evidence: CPJ I 132 (164 BCE), a letter from the dioiketes Herodes to the Jew Onias found in the Serapeum archive near Memphis, because Onias was probably strategos of the Heliopolite nome (Wilcken), not a Memphis resident.

3rd c. BCE (midpoint c. -250; the Berlin museum database dates the stela to c. 203 BCE, but that date was not checked here). The bilingual funerary stela of Chahap son of Paneith (Berlin 2118), an army chief of the Matoi and a notable Memphite of Phoenician origin, includes among his priestly titles 'scribe of the divine records in the granary of the chief artificer in the district of the Jews'. Szántó argues that this 'undoubtedly confirms the existence of a Jewish quarter' and that 'a Jewish quarter existed in Ptolemaic Memphis similarly to the Greek, the Ionian and Idumean ethnic quarters'. Its location is unknown. Vittmann instead links the place with the Jewish Camp (Castra Iudaeorum) in the southern Delta, a view Szántó rejects. This suggests an organized Jewish quarter (community) in Memphis. No size is given.

Late Period and Ptolemaic period (Ptolemaic midpoint 332-30 BCE = c. -181). Getty publication 'Mediterranean Encounters' (Egypt and the Classical World): Memphis's population 'included Phoenicians, Greeks (Hellenomemphites), Carians (Caro-Memphites), Syrians, Persians, and Jews', many probably first garrisoned there as mercenaries. It cites Jakobeit 2016, 'Das jüdische Viertel Yht in Memphis - ein weiterer Beleg', as a further attestation of a Jewish quarter (Yht) in Memphis. This indicates an ethnic Jewish quarter or community. No figures are given.

Ptolemaic period (332-30 BCE; midpoint c. -181). Dominic Rathbone's review (LRB 1990) of D. J. Thompson, Memphis under the Ptolemies, summarizes Thompson's findings: apart from Egyptians and Greeks, the city's population 'contained Phoenician, Carian, Jewish and Idumaean communities'. This is a scholarly assessment of a Jewish community in Ptolemaic Memphis. No size is given.

First half of the 1st c. BCE (midpoint c. -75). CPJ I 141, a Greek papyrus letter from Memphis (reinterpreted by R. Rémondon, 'Les anti-Sémites de Memphis', CdE 35, 1960), asks the dioiketes to give a priest the same lodging as Artemidoros 'for you know that they are nauseated by Jews' (oidas gar hoti bdelussontai Ioudaious). Szántó treats it as the earliest Greek documentary evidence of anti-Jewish feeling and places it in 'the international environment of Memphis'. This implies that Jews were present in Memphis and suggests local hostility. No numbers are given.

Event, 47 BCE. Josephus, Antiquities 14.8.1 (14.132), on the campaign of Mithridates of Pergamum and Antipater to relieve Caesar: 'when the Jews about Memphis heard that these Jews were come over to Caesar, they also invited Mithridates', who enlisted them into his army. This is an ancient literary attestation of Jews living in or around Memphis (the phrase may cover the Memphis district rather than the city alone). No number is given.
